questions.question: Why is Egeon condemned to death when he arrives in Ephesus?

options.text: The city's law forbids Syracusian visitors unless ransomed.
He has stolen the goldsmith's unfinished chain.
He has tried to take the Duke's place as ruler.
He has refused to recognize Adriana as his wife.

questions.explanation: Hostility between the cities makes Egeon's arrival punishable by death unless a ransom is raised.

evidence.exact:
DUKE.
Merchant of Syracusa, plead no more.
I am not partial to infringe our laws.
The enmity and discord which of late
Sprung from the rancorous outrage of your Duke
To merchants, our well-dealing countrymen,
Who, wanting guilders to redeem their lives,
Have seal’d his rigorous statutes with their bloods,
Excludes all pity from our threat’ning looks.
For since the mortal and intestine jars
’Twixt thy seditious countrymen and us,
It hath in solemn synods been decreed,
Both by the Syracusians and ourselves,
To admit no traffic to our adverse towns;
Nay more, if any born at Ephesus
Be seen at Syracusian marts and fairs;
Again, if any Syracusian born
Come to the bay of Ephesus, he dies,
His goods confiscate to the Duke’s dispose,
Unless a thousand marks be levied
To quit the penalty and to ransom him.
Thy substance, valued at the highest rate,
Cannot amount unto a hundred marks;
Therefore by law thou art condemn’d to die.

questions.question: What brings Antipholus of Syracuse on his travels?

options.text: An order to recover a stolen gold chain.
The search for his lost mother and brother.
A commission to arrest the Duke of Ephesus.
A promise to marry Adriana's servant.

questions.explanation: Antipholus describes losing himself while seeking his missing mother and brother.

evidence.exact:
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE.
He that commends me to mine own content
Commends me to the thing I cannot get.
I to the world am like a drop of water
That in the ocean seeks another drop,
Who, failing there to find his fellow forth,
Unseen, inquisitive, confounds himself.
So I, to find a mother and a brother,
In quest of them, unhappy, lose myself.

questions.question: What precaution does the Merchant advise Antipholus of Syracuse to take?

options.text: Leave all his money with the Duke's jailer.
Buy a gold chain before finding an inn.
Say he comes from Epidamnum rather than Syracuse.
Pretend to be Adriana's husband before entering town.

questions.explanation: The Merchant warns him to conceal his Syracusian origin to avoid confiscation and punishment.

evidence.exact:
MERCHANT.
Therefore give out you are of Epidamnum,
Lest that your goods too soon be confiscate.
This very day a Syracusian merchant
Is apprehended for arrival here,
And, not being able to buy out his life,
According to the statute of the town
Dies ere the weary sun set in the west.
There is your money that I had to keep.

questions.question: Why does Adriana take Antipholus of Syracuse home with her?

options.text: She recognizes him as her husband's lost brother.
She hires him to find the missing goldsmith.
She wants him to ransom Egeon before sunset.
She mistakes him for her husband.

questions.explanation: Adriana addresses the visiting twin as her husband, while he wonders whether he is dreaming.

evidence.exact:
ADRIANA.
How ill agrees it with your gravity
To counterfeit thus grossly with your slave,
Abetting him to thwart me in my mood;
Be it my wrong, you are from me exempt,
But wrong not that wrong with a more contempt.
Come, I will fasten on this sleeve of thine.
Thou art an elm, my husband, I a vine,
Whose weakness, married to thy stronger state,
Makes me with thy strength to communicate:
If aught possess thee from me, it is dross,
Usurping ivy, brier, or idle moss,
Who all, for want of pruning, with intrusion
Infect thy sap, and live on thy confusion.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE.
To me she speaks; she moves me for her theme.
What, was I married to her in my dream?
Or sleep I now, and think I hear all this?
What error drives our eyes and ears amiss?
Until I know this sure uncertainty
I’ll entertain the offer’d fallacy.

questions.question: How does Antipholus of Ephesus react when he is shut out of his own house?

options.text: He decides to dine elsewhere and give his hostess the chain.
He leaves Ephesus immediately without his servant.
He asks the Abbess to marry him to Luciana.
He forgives the household and sends everyone gifts.

questions.explanation: Angered by the closed doors, he plans dinner at the Porpentine and a gift meant to spite his wife.

evidence.exact:
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS.
You have prevail’d. I will depart in quiet,
And, in despite of mirth, mean to be merry.
I know a wench of excellent discourse,
Pretty and witty; wild, and yet, too, gentle;
There will we dine. This woman that I mean,
My wife (but, I protest, without desert)
Hath oftentimes upbraided me withal;
To her will we to dinner.—Get you home
And fetch the chain, by this I know ’tis made.
Bring it, I pray you, to the Porpentine,
For there’s the house. That chain will I bestow
(Be it for nothing but to spite my wife)
Upon mine hostess there. Good sir, make haste.
Since mine own doors refuse to entertain me,
I’ll knock elsewhere, to see if they’ll disdain me.

She believes he is her sister's husband.
She knows he is already married to the Abbess.

questions.question: Why does Pinch order Antipholus of Ephesus and his servant to be bound?

options.text: He mistakes their confused protests for demonic possession.
He has discovered that they plan to murder the Duke.
He wants to force them to confess they are from Syracuse.
He has been asked to take them away to sea as sailors.

questions.explanation: Pinch diagnoses both master and servant as possessed and orders confinement in a dark room.

evidence.exact:
PINCH.
Mistress, both man and master is possess’d,
I know it by their pale and deadly looks.
They must be bound and laid in some dark room.

questions.question: What does the Abbess reveal when the two sets of twins finally meet?

options.text: She raised both Antipholuses together in Ephesus.
She is Emilia, Egeon's wife and the twins' mother.
She is Adriana's mother and Angelo's business partner.
She arranged the gold-chain confusion to test the Duke.

questions.explanation: The Abbess identifies herself as the Emilia who bore Egeon's two sons, reuniting the separated family.

evidence.exact:
ABBESS.
Whoever bound him, I will loose his bonds,
And gain a husband by his liberty.
Speak, old Egeon, if thou be’st the man
That hadst a wife once called Emilia,
That bore thee at a burden two fair sons.
O, if thou be’st the same Egeon, speak,
And speak unto the same Emilia!
